Transcript body:
[00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Priya, I'm the account lead for Redwood for Cobalt Retail. Mark from our engineering team will jump in on benchmarks and the kernel mapping later. Jenna, Marta, Ravi, you able to hear ok?
[00:08] Jenna: Yep good, thanks. Audio's fine.
[00:11] Marta: all good here.
[00:15] Priya: Awesome. Quick agenda: console catalog demo, how to read bench outputs, and then we can talk deployment paths — hosted, dedicated, private — and security. We'll leave 10 mins at the end for logistics and next steps. Sound good?
[00:26] Jenna: Perfect. We're mainly interested in personalization latency and cost. We have a 120ms token target for the chat microservice, and heavy daily volume. Also strong need for VPC and KMS.
[00:37] Priya: Got it. Mark, want to take the console and bench walkthrough?
[00:40] Mark: Sure. I'm going to share my screen — lemme know if the deck comes through.
[00:45] [screen share begins]
[00:48] Mark: Alright, so this is the Redwood Console — the model catalog page. On the left we have filters: model family, sequence length, quantization support, and hardware compatibility. Notice we label models as "verified fit" for common inference patterns.
[01:06] Marta: How precise is the "verified" label? Like does it mean we've run a full production bench?
[01:12] Mark: Good question. Verified means we've run our standard bench suite at a couple of sequence lengths and common kernels. It's not exhaustive exhaustive but it's a reliable signal. For full production we recommend a short bench run on your workload, which we can help scope.
[01:25] Priya: And we provide the bench CSV output which maps to latency percentiles, token throughput, and selected kernel — that CSV is what we'll share.
[01:33] Jenna: Can you show an example of that CSV and how to read it?
[01:36] Mark: Yup. Switching to the bench results tab. Here you can see rows per model variant — quantized variants, float16, etc. Columns include median latency, p95 p99, throughput (tok/s), and the recommended kernel or kernel combo. Some rows show a note "auto-batch friendly" or "KV cache optimized".
[01:55] [00:58] Ravi: Sorry to interrupt — when you say kernel can you clarify? Do you mean the GPU kernel selection inside your runtime?
[02:03] Mark: Exactly. Kernel here is the low-level compute kernel we choose — e.g., Triton style fused attention kernel, or an optimized GEMM path. Different models and sequence lengths favor different kernels. We surfaced that in the column called "Runtime Kernel" — sometimes transcription shows it as "run-time kernel" or even mis-typed as "run kernel" in older exports.
[02:20] Jenna: Ok. For our personalization use-case we do many short turn chitchat sequences, so KV cache behavior matters a lot. Do you show cache hit/miss impact?
[02:29] Mark: We do a KV cache sensitivity test in our bench: same prompt prefix, then repeated incremental tokens to measure per-token latency improvements. In the CSV you'll see a delta column that shows benefit with prefix caching. Sometimes the transcriptions or labels come out as "K-V cash" in internal notes — sorry for the typo, that's a common transcription artifact.
[02:45] Marta: Ha, noted.
[02:47] Priya: Another important piece — compatibility matrix. We map models to recommended hardware: A100 variants, H100, or M10/M60 class for cloud vendors. In the console you can export a compatibility matrix that shows which quantizations are supported on which hardware and which kernels we pick.
[03:06] Jenna: Do you cover int8 quantization? We tried a third-party quant tool, but output quality dropped for our domain.
[03:14] Mark: We surface quantization recommendations per workload type. For chat style short sequences often int8 works well but you need to validate on your prompt set. That's where Redwood Optimize comes in — it suggests quant profiles and flags quality regressions based on eval sets.
[03:29] Ravi: Quick infra question: if we start on hosted for speed, can we later move to Dedicated without code changes?
[03:36] Priya: Yes that's a core promise — the same API and routing layer. You can pin model versions and deployment policies. Moving from hosted to Dedicated is mostly a config/ops change, not an API rewrite.
[03:47] Marta: And Private (VPC/on-prem) — how different is that operationally?
[03:52] Mark: Private requires network and KMS integration; the control plane is private and we can provide an on-prem package. There are a few differences: startup times, patching window, and we hand over more of the runtime ops to your infra team. But the console UI and APIs remain consistent.
[04:12] Jenna: Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, audit logs — are these available for Dedicated and Private?
[04:19] Priya: Yes. We offer SOC 2 Type II compliance for our hosted plane, and Dedicated/Private include audit log forwarding, SSO, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. I'll attach the security pack after the call.
[04:33] Marta: Can you point to the security doc right now?
[04:35] Priya: Sure — I'll drop the link in the follow-up. We avoid posting full PDFs in the transcript but it's in the packet we'll share.
[04:43] Jenna: Great. Back to bench interpretation — what thresholds would indicate we need Dedicated vs Hosted? For us, steady-state daily throughput is 1.5M tokens and spikes double that.
[04:54] Mark: We look at three things: token throughput per GPU for the model+quant profile, latency SLO headroom at p95, and cost per 1k tokens. If your peak is sustained and latency headroom shrinks, Dedicated is better for predictable latency. Hosted is great for unpredictable spikes because of multi-tenant burst capacity, but cost can be higher at scale.
[05:15] Ravi: Do you have a calculator?
[05:17] Priya: Yes — Mark will share a sizing spreadsheet. The quick rule: if you have predictable sustained utilization above commit thresholds (we discuss commits for Dedicated), you likely save money on Dedicated. We'll provide sample numbers.
[05:28] Mark: Also note the route-level controls — you can set a policy that routes low-priority requests to an economical quantized variant and high-priority to a low-latency float16 model. That lets you hit cost targets without losing SLAs for priority flows.
[05:43] Jenna: I like that. Can the console show that routing split simulation?
[05:47] Mark: We have a basic visualization in Console under "Routing" — it's a simulated traffic pie and expected p95 cost/latency. For deeper analysis we run benched simulations offline.
[05:58] Marta: About the bench CSV — will it include sample prompts and the exact runtime flags used? We need to reproduce the test locally.
[06:06] Mark: The CSV includes the prompt seed set id, the actual prompt filenames (or hash), sequence length, batch size, kernel used, and runtime flags like batch horizon and kv cache enable. If you need the exact runtime command we can include that too.
[06:20] Jenna: Excellent. On evals — can Redwood Optimize run regression checks against our retail test set? We have a custom labelled set for hallucination and pricing errors.
[06:31] Priya: Yes. Redwood Optimize supports hooking your evals — we can set thresholds and alert when quality drops post-quantization or kernel changes. We can integrate with your s3 bucket for eval artifacts.
[06:42] Ravi: Regarding data residency — some customers need EU-only processing. Is that possible on hosted?
[06:48] Priya: We have region pins for hosted — you can restrict a route to EU regions. For stricter residency and control, Private/VPC is the recommended path.
[06:58] Marta: Competitors question — we trialed Bedrock but felt it was harder to get consistent latency across models. How do you make latency predictable?
[07:08] Mark: A few levers: kernel selection tuned per model/seq len, batch scheduling with tight SLO-aware batching, and prefix caching. We also enforce backpressure and have fallback routes. Predictability comes from the Dedicated config and our autoscaling policies which prioritize latency SLOs over throughput when requested.
[07:27] Jenna: Any gotchas with quantized models and tokenization? We had issues where tokenizers changed subtly and broke caching in a previous setup.
[07:36] Mark: Tokenization mismatches cause cache misses; we recommend pinning tokenizer versions and validating the KV hash. Console export includes tokenizer checksum. We also support SDK-side utilities to normalize tokenization.
[07:48] [08:00] Marta: Could you walk us through a short scenario — say we have a 30k daily active users generating 20 tokens per request average, and we want 120ms p95 — what would you recommend?
[08:11] Mark: Let me sketch it quick. At 30k DAU * 20 tokens average you get 600k tokens/day — but what's important is concurrency and p95 behaviour. If you have peak concurrency of 50 requests/sec, you need to look at tok/s per GPU for the chosen model. If we pick a quantized 7B variant that does 6k tok/s on A100, you'd need less than one GPU, but latency depends on batch horizon. For low latency we keep batch sizes small and rely on autoscale or Dedicated pools to meet p95.
[08:41] Jenna: That helps. For our case, peaks are around 120 rps for checkout personalization flows for 10 minutes after promos.
[08:50] Mark: Short spikes like that are where hosted with burst capacity shines unless you want to carve a Dedicated pool for promos. We can also set route-based autoscaling to temporarily bump capacity.
[09:01] Ravi: Is there a soft limit on how many dedicated pools you can have? We have several teams that might want isolated pools.
[09:08] Priya: We typically provision multiple pools for enterprise customers; it's a sizing play. Dedicated is priced per pool and capacity. We'll include recommended pool counts in the spreadsheet.
[09:18] Marta: Great. Quick question on monitoring — do you provide token-level cost attribution by route?
[09:24] Mark: Yes, Console exposes token-level cost breakdown, latency histograms, and per-route traces. You can also hook sampling-based traces into your observability provider.
[09:33] Jenna: We'd like to run a pilot — scope is: two routes (personalization chat + fallback reranker), sample prompt set, bench it, and a 2-week canary on hosted with routing policies. Is that feasible?
[09:45] Priya: Totally. That aligns with our typical pilot. We'll produce a pilot plan: bench, sizing, plan for routing split, and a canary run.
[09:54] Mark: For the reranker, note that batching is important — rerankers often get very high token fanouts; we can show suggested batch sizes and quant choices to avoid latency blowups.
[10:06] [10:20] Jenna: One more thing — how do you handle fallback when a model is busy? For ex, fallback to smaller model but keep quality?
[10:28] Mark: We support canary and fallback policies: route-level fallback to a cheaper quantized model or to a cached response. There is also the ability to run a quick lightweight model for initial tokens then swap to larger models, but swapping mid-response has complexities with KV cache warming.
[10:45] Jenna: Interesting. Could you show us an example fallback policy in Console?
[10:51] Mark: Sure — switching screens. Here's a route config: primary model x, fallback model y, p95 latency threshold, and ride-through policy that diverts 30% of traffic when primary p95 exceeds threshold. The Console sim then shows expected p95 and cost delta.
[11:12] Marta: What about instrumentation of fallback events? We need visibility when fallbacks happen for product QA.
[11:18] Mark: We emit events to audit logs and metrics; Console surfaces counts and you can forward them to your monitoring stack.
[11:26] Ravi: Security again — can audit logs be forwarded to our SIEM?
[11:30] Priya: Yes, syslog or S3 export or streaming through a partner connector. For Private deployments you can keep logs entirely within your VPC.
[11:40] Marta: Any immediate blockers we should be aware of for a pilot?
[11:44] Mark: On our side, just access to your prompt set and sample traffic pattern. On your side, if you need private connectivity or KMS we will scope the network work. Nothing else heavy.
[11:55] Jenna: Ok, timeline wise we want to start benching next week and run a canary in two weeks. Is that realistic?
[12:01] Priya: Yes. We'll prepare the bench plan and bench CSV by Monday/Tuesday.
[12:06] Mark: Also, note that for certain models kernel selection may vary on H100 vs A100; benches need to include both if you want cross-hardware guarantees.
[12:17] Ravi: We're primarily on AWS, A100 in us-west-2. We'll include that in the prompt.
[12:22] Priya: Great. Any final questions?
[12:25] Marta: One small thing — pricing: do you charge for bench runs?
[12:29] Priya: Bench runs for pilots are complimentary; production benching at large scale is scoped. We'll include the pricing tiers in the follow-up.
[12:37] Jenna: Perfect.
[12:40] [wrap-up] Priya: Ok quick recap — Mark will share bench CSV and kernel map (action item), I'll send Dedicated vs Hosted cost spreadsheet and security pack, Jenna will share sample prompts and traffic profile. We'll aim to reconvene after bench results for a short technical review.
[12:57] Jenna: Thanks everyone. This was helpful.
[13:00] Priya: Thanks, talk soon.
